title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Marine
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: Cyberattack forces a systems-wide outage at North Carolina Ports, slowing gate and terminal operations
items.content_text: North Carolina Ports confirmed a cyberattack that triggered a systems-wide outage across its facilities — the Port of Wilmington, the Port of Morehead City and the Charlotte Inland Port — detected on 4 August and disrupting operations into 5 August. The authority told customers that gates would open late and that delays should be expected while it worked to contain and recover. The confirmed impact is IT-side: an outage of the systems that run gate and terminal processing rather than any reported manipulation of cranes or other control systems. But the operational effect on cargo flow was real, and it lands a confirmed disruption at a US port during the window. North Carolina Ports engaged the state DOT, the state IT department and the US Coast Guard; the threat actor and whether data was stolen had not been disclosed as of this edition.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: North Carolina Ports notice / The Maritime Executive

items.title: Qilin ransomware gang claims the Shipping Association of New York & New Jersey
items.content_text: The Russian-speaking Qilin ransomware crew listed the Shipping Association of New York & New Jersey (SANYNJ) on its dark-web leak site on 8 June, with the entry updated into July. SANYNJ represents the terminal operators, ocean carriers, stevedores and marine-related businesses that move cargo and employ longshore workers across the busiest port complex on the US East Coast, so a compromise there reaches deep into port labour and logistics data. Qilin published few details and the sample-data link was broken at the time of reporting, so this is a claim rather than a confirmed breach, and no operational disruption to terminals has been reported. Treat it as a prompt to verify defences at maritime associations and their member operators.

items.title: Resecurity details Anubis ransomware breach of Ancona’s Adriatic port authority
items.content_text: Resecurity published analysis on 11 June of an Anubis ransomware attack on the Central Adriatic Sea Port Authority, which runs the Italian port of Ancona. The intrusion — dated to December 2025 and claimed by Anubis in January — began with a spear-phishing email against port-management staff and moved laterally through insecure Office 365 and Azure cloud accounts; the attackers worked purely through IT weaknesses and did not need to touch operational technology. Stolen material reportedly included contracts, employee records and port safety and security plans, with a $10 million ransom demand. The authority characterised most of the data as public or soon-to-be-public and put overall loss near 2%, but the case shows how an IT-side compromise at a port can still reach sensitive safety and security documentation.

items.title: King Ocean Services discloses data breach at Caribbean/Latin America ocean carrier
items.content_text: Miami-based ocean carrier and logistics firm King Ocean Services disclosed on 11 July a data-security incident that exposed personal information, including government ID numbers, of affected individuals. King Ocean provides ocean transportation, trucking and warehousing across the Caribbean, Central and South America. The company has not detailed the cause, timeline or whether a third party was involved. The confirmed impact is IT/data-side rather than vessel or terminal OT, but it underlines that maritime logistics operators remain squarely in attackers' sights.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: King Ocean Services breach notice / ISSSource

items.title: Leaked Fortinet firewall credentials expose maritime, port and energy networks
items.content_text: Threat-intelligence reporting in early July flagged a “FortiBleed” exposure — large sets of leaked Fortinet firewall credentials — affecting maritime, port and energy organisations. For ports and shipping companies, Fortinet gear typically sits on the perimeter and the remote-access path used by shore-side IT and, increasingly, vessel connectivity. Valid credentials to that edge are a direct route toward the OT and logistics systems behind it, and they sidestep the need for an exploit entirely.

items.title: Federal alert: Iran-affiliated hackers manipulating the PLCs that also run port and terminal OT
items.content_text: Federal agencies sharpened their warning that Iran-affiliated hackers are actively manipulating the programmable logic controllers behind US critical infrastructure — the same controllers that run cranes, fuel, power and water systems inside MTSA-regulated ports and terminals. Advisory AA26-097A, updated 22 July, describes actors reaching internet-exposed Rockwell, Schneider and Siemens gear, stealing project files, and rewriting or deleting control logic, in some cases disabling shutdown and alarm functions without alerting operators. Port facilities are exactly the mixed IT/OT environment the campaign favours: diverse controllers, remote maintenance access and edge devices often reachable from the internet. The activity has caused operational disruption and financial loss across critical-infrastructure sectors. It is opportunistic rather than sophisticated — the way in is weak credentials and exposed controllers, not a novel exploit.

items.title: Researchers find remote-access flaws in NAVTOR NavBox vessel OT gateway (now patched)
items.content_text: Maritime-security firm Cydome disclosed three vulnerabilities in the NAVTOR NavBox, an onboard gateway that manages navigation and network operations and sits at the IT/OT boundary on many vessels. In version 4.12.0.3, missing authentication on HTTP API endpoints (CVE-2026-2752), a path-traversal flaw (CVE-2026-2753) and an information-disclosure issue (CVE-2026-2754) could allow unauthorised remote access to vessel telemetry, network configuration and sensitive operational data such as ECDIS IP addresses. NavTor acknowledged the findings, confirmed they were fixed in later releases (v4.14.1.2 and v4.16.2.4) and notified affected customers. It is a research finding with no reported in-the-wild exploitation, but it is a rare, concrete look at how a shipboard OT gateway can expose navigation systems.

items.title: USCG cyber report: maritime incidents up 17% and OT now in the majority of missions
items.content_text: The US Coast Guard Cyber Command’s fifth annual Cyber Trends and Insights in the Marine Environment (CTIME) report finds reported maritime cyber incidents rose about 17% year over year, with phishing still the leading entry point and operational technology increasingly central — OT featured in 62% of CGCYBER cyber missions, up from 46% the year before. The report stresses that resilience depends less on new tooling than on fundamentals: secured terminal operating systems, enforced MFA, incident reporting and continuity planning. The through-line for operators is that OT is now squarely in scope, and basic hygiene still closes most of the gap.

items.title: GNSS interference and GPS spoofing persist as a daily hazard in the Gulf and Strait of Hormuz
items.content_text: GPS and GNSS interference has continued as a near-daily hazard for shipping through the Arabian Gulf, Strait of Hormuz and Gulf of Oman across 2026, with vessels reporting false positions — some placed over airports or on dry land — and degraded AIS integrity amid sustained regional tension. Maritime security centres advise that navigation systems in the region should be treated as potentially unreliable and that crews fall back on radar and visual methods. This is electronic-warfare interference rather than a network intrusion, but it degrades the position, timing and AIS data that bridge and terminal systems depend on — and the timing feeds inside OT need hardening too.

items.title: Cisco Secure FMC zero-day exploited — the edge that fronts port and vessel networks
items.content_text: Cisco disclosed CVE-2026-20316, a static (hard-coded) credential flaw in the web interface of Secure Firewall Management Center (FMC) that is being exploited as a zero-day. An unauthenticated remote attacker can log in with a built-in low-privileged account and read sensitive data, and Cisco warns it can be chained with other FMC bugs to escalate privileges. CISA added it to the KEV catalog on 29 July with a 1 August federal remediation deadline. FMC manages the firewalls that sit on the perimeter and remote-access path in front of many port, terminal and vessel-shore networks, so a foothold there is a foothold toward the OT behind it. CVSS is only 5.3, but active exploitation makes it urgent.

_otthreatfeed.date_note: Added to KEV 29 Jul 2026 — actively exploited

items.title: CISA flags API flaws in iDirect iQ-Series satellite terminals used across maritime VSAT
items.content_text: CISA advisory ICSA-26-183-01 covers vulnerabilities in ST Engineering iDirect iQ-Series satellite terminals — hardware widely deployed for maritime, energy and defense VSAT connectivity. The lead flaw, CVE-2026-38059 (CVSS 7.5 v3 / 8.7 v4), exposes the terminal’s REST management API without authentication, letting an attacker on the network read the device ID, MAC, firmware version and — critically — the Terminal Private Key identifier used for satellite-network authentication, opening the door to terminal impersonation and reconnaissance. A companion CSRF gap on the reboot endpoint lets a state-changing request through on a session cookie alone. iDirect has released fixed firmware 4.5.2.2. For vessels and offshore assets, this is the satcom link itself.

items.title: USCG Marine Transportation System cyber rule: reporting and Cyber Security Officer duties in force
items.content_text: The US Coast Guard's Marine Transportation System cybersecurity rule continues to phase in for US ports and MTSA-regulated facilities. Reportable cyber incidents must be reported to the National Response Center (within 12 hours for incidents affecting seaworthiness or security compliance), and facilities must designate a Cyber Security Officer alongside the traditional Facility Security Officer. For operators the near-term work is governance: named accountability, incident-reporting playbooks, and a cyber plan that maps to the rule.

_otthreatfeed.date_note: Rule in force since 16 Jul 2025 — phased compliance

items.title: IACS UR E26/E27 keep raising the cyber bar for newbuild vessels
items.content_text: The IACS Unified Requirements UR E26 (whole-ship cyber resilience) and UR E27 (equipment-level security) apply to vessels with construction contracts signed on or after 1 July 2024, covering identification, protection, detection, response and recovery across integrated IT/OT and third-party equipment. The requirements shift cyber resilience into ship design and supplier obligations, so owners, yards and integrators building 500 GT-plus tonnage need cyber baked into specifications, not bolted on later.
